query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the HVAF-i7 process to achieve a higher in‐flight particle velocity—by adjusting the spray distance to the 300–350 mm range—will improve the deposition efficiency and thus yield a thicker, well‐adherent FeCoNiCrAl bond coat without compromising its low oxidation and high-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy feedstock with a particle size of 15–45 μm, as used in previous HVAF-M3 studies.
generation.intervention: Change the HVAF-i7 spraying parameters by setting the stand-off (spray) distance to approximately 300–350 mm to increase particle velocity during deposition.
generation.conditions: Deposition using the HVAF-i7 torch on substrates (including those with internal diameters as small as 120 mm) under conditions typical for high-temperature thermal-barrier service; other parameters remain controlled as in the baseline process.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy upon impact leads to improved splat flattening, bonding, and a reduction in re-splash or porosity.
generation.mechanism: Higher particle velocity increases the momentum of incoming particles, which improves their deformation and adhesion upon substrate impact. This results in a higher deposition efficiency, yielding a thicker coating while maintaining low as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the overall bond-coat thickness compared to the baseline HVAF-i7 process conditions using 15–45 μm feedstock, while retaining high coating integrity and minimal oxidation.
generation.baseline: HVAF-i7 deposition of FeCoNiCrAl coatings with 15–45 μm feedstock that produces acceptable quality but with inadequate thickness.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is expected to hold as long as the increase in particle velocity (via the adjusted spray distance) does not induce excessive oxidation or compromise coating adhesion. The results must also remain consistent for deposition in confined geometries (minimum 120 mm internal diameters).
generation.uncertainty: Exact tuning of the stand-off distance and any necessary adjustments to fuel/oxygen flow rates specific to the HVAF-i7 torch may require further optimization to match the deposition performance observed with the M3 system.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of HVAF-i7 deposition experiments on FeCoNiCrAl coatings using the same 15–45 μm feedstock, varying only the stand-off distance (e.g., 250 mm, 300 mm, and 350 mm). Measure the in-flight particle velocity and deposition efficiency under each condition while ensuring that other parameters (e.g., fuel/oxygen flow rates) remain constant.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the stand-off distance to the 300–350 mm range does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (without degrading microstructure, adhesion, or increasing oxidation) relative to the baseline condition, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

To date, in addition to traditional casting and forging methods, various thermal spraying techniques have been employed to coat HEAs on the substrate, firstly, high-velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF) [,] technique in which a specially designed torch allows the compressed flame to expand freely consuming the gases combustion, such as Hydrocarbon’s, i.e., Methane (CH4), Propane (C3H6), Butane (C4H8) or kerosene oil type liquid fuels. O2 and fuel are mixed in the combustion zone under conditions that display the correct combustion mode and pressure []. This process generates a very high-velocity flame which is used to propel the particles at near-supersonic speeds before making an impact on the substrate [].
